extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical philosophy and moral theory
extracted.subtask_description: Close conceptual account of virtues (reserve, jocularity, shame, self-control) and an extended analytic taxonomy of Justice and Injustice, including distributive and corrective forms and their respective standards of proportion and equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration versus Reserve versus Truthfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes three character-types: Exaggerators (who assume boastful qualities to gain advantage), the Reserved (who depreciate their own qualities and thus appear refined), and the Truthful Man (the mean opposed to Exaggeration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggerators pretend to qualities useful to others and therefore are common and blameworthy; the Reserved who moderate their reserve (especially in non-obvious truths) give an impression of refinement. Excess and extreme deficiency both partake of Exaggeration (e.g., excessive plainness of dress). Avoid both boasting for gain and excessive, conspicuous self-deprecation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factotum (false small-claimant) as a fault
rubrics_metrics.description: People who falsely lay claim to small or obvious things are called Factotums and are despicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boasting about modest or easily-checked skills is an anti-pattern; credibility is undermined by petty false claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jocularity: Buffoon, Clownish, and the Man of Tact
rubrics_metrics.description: Jocularity admits excess (Buffoon), defect (Clownish/Stern), and a mean (Tact). Buffoons aim at laughter at any cost and offend; Clownish persons refuse jesting and are socially unhelpful; the man of Tact says and listens to what is fit for a gentleman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good jocularity (Tact) requires saying and tolerating what is becoming for a good man, avoiding hurting the object of wit, and fitting manners to education and social position (old vs new comedy distinction). Excess (rude, indiscriminate jokery) and deficiency (hostility to any jest) are both faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decency as a standard for jocularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes vulgar jocularity (obscene in old comedy) from gentlemanly innuendo (new comedy); decency is a governing standard for what is fit to say or hear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate jocularity by audience, education, and social norms; some scurrility may be legally forbidden and the refined person is 'a law to himself' in limiting acceptable jesting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shame is a feeling, not a virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Shame is defined as 'a kind of fear of disgrace' and resembles a physical feeling; it is not properly a moral virtue because it functions as a check on youthful passions rather than marking the good man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shame is praise-worthy for the young as a corrective; however, for a mature good person it indicates having committed or being disposed to disgraceful acts, and so is not to be treated as a full virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-control as a mixed state (not a full virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-control (continence) is 'a kind of mixed state' rather than a pure virtue; its full treatment is deferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize degrees between feelings and virtues; self-control has moral relevance but is conceptually distinct from the virtues properly so-called.

rubrics_metrics.name: General definition of Justice and Injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is a moral state in virtue of which people have the capacity and disposition to do what is just and to wish it; Injustice is the contrary state leading to unjust action and desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as the baseline: Justice concerns right action toward others and Injustice concerns acting against proportionate or lawful standards in dealings with others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple senses of Just/Unjust (lawful, grasping, unequal)
rubrics_metrics.description: The terms 'Just' and 'Unjust' are used in several senses: one set refers to lawful vs unlawful; another to grasping (seeking more than one's share) vs non-grasping; another to equality vs inequality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing a case, determine which sense is operative (legal, distributive/equal shares, or grasping-for-gain) before applying the relevant standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular Injustice distinct from vice-coextensive injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a particular kind of Injustice that is not simply co-extensive with all Vice: it specifically involves grasping for gain in dealings with others and can be distinguished from vices like cowardice or intemperance which may produce unjust acts without constituting the same species of Injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify wrongful acts: ask whether the vice primarily explains the conduct (e.g., lust, cowardice) or whether the act is specifically unjust because of seeking illicit gain or violating dealings with others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species of Particular Justice: Distributive and Corrective
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular Justice has two species: Distributive (concerned with distributions of honour, wealth, etc.) and Corrective (concerned with rectifying transactions between persons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply distributive rules when allocating shares of common goods; apply corrective rules when remedying gains and losses arising from voluntary or involuntary transactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributive Justice: proportionality (geometrical proportion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distributive Justice is proportionate: the Just is that distribution in which shares stand in the same proportion to one another as the corresponding merits or contributions (A:B::C:D). The equal here is a mean and involves at least four terms (persons and things).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the relevant 'rate' (merit, need, birth, wealth, virtue) for proportion; equality is preserved only when shares conform to that chosen proportion. Different political groups may contest which rate to use (democrats, oligarchs, aristocrats).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrective Justice: arithmetical equality between loss and gain
rubrics_metrics.description: Corrective Justice aims at restoring equality between parties by making the result of a transaction equal to what it was before (a mean between loss and gain). The judge's office is to take from the greater and give to the lesser to re-establish equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In disputes, treat parties as previously equal and measure injury in terms of gain and loss; remedies should neutralize unjust advantage, restoring parties to equal footing (arithmetical rather than proportionate standard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the Judge as personification of the Just (mesidios)
rubrics_metrics.description: The judge is conceived as the middle-man whose duty is to hit the mean by making the unequal equal again; the judge's function is to determine and apply the corrective mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate adjudication by whether the remedy restores proportional/arithmetic equality appropriate to the species of justice at issue; consider voluntariness/involuntariness of acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocation as a necessary but insufficient standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple reciprocation (Tit-for-tat) is not a full account of Justice; reciprocation must be according to proportion, not mere exact equality, and voluntariness/involuntariness and status differences affect what reciprocity requires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In exchanges, insist on proportionate reciprocation (quality- and quantity-adjusted), not blind equality; recognize exceptions (authority relations, punishments) where simple reciprocity fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Money and commensurability as enabling just exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: All exchange requires comparability; money functions as a common measure (νόμισμα) by making diverse goods commensurable and so allowing proportionate reciprocity and exchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing justice in economic transactions, identify whether commensurability (price/measure) has been established; lack of a common measure prevents proper equalisation and fair exchange.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand (mutual want) as the bond of exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: Exchange occurs only when parties want what the other has; Demand is the common bond enabling exchange and thus the possibility of proportionate reciprocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a purported exchange is voluntary and mutually desired; without reciprocal demand, there is no genuine exchange to which justice rules of reciprocity apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as a mean with a distinctive character
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is a mean, but in a distinct way from other virtues: it aims at producing the mean (proportionate equality) between extremes (excess and defect), whereas Injustice occupies the extremes themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge actions by whether they aim to secure or violate proportionate equality; justice produces balanced relations rather than merely intermediate personal dispositions.
